headline: A Chambermaid's Hungry Bite Solved a Century-Old Diamond Heist
meta_description: In 1926, a Paris cleaning lady bit into a stolen apple and discovered the legendary Grand Condé diamond, solving a high-profile museum heist from the Château d…
summary_short: A hungry chambermaid in 1926 Paris bit into an apple from a guest's suitcase and discovered a pink gemstone lodged inside—solving the case of a famous diamond theft.
body:
In 1926, Parisian chambermaid Suzanne Schiltz was cleaning hotel rooms when hunger got the better of her. She took an apple from a guest's suitcase and bit into it—only to feel her teeth strike something impossibly hard. Staring down in shock, she found a pink gemstone the size of a lima bean embedded in the fruit. That single bite solved one of the era's most audacious heists: the theft of the Grand Condé diamond from the Château de Chantilly, located roughly 30 miles north of Paris. Two amateur thieves had stolen the diamond and 74 other pieces of jewelry using nothing more than a ladder, but their success ended there. Valued at $3 million in 1920s dollars, they had managed to sell only a fraction of the haul because jewelers and pawnbrokers refused to touch items as famous and identifiable as the Grand Condé.

According to newspaper accounts from the time, police confronted one burglar with a clever riddle: "Do you like apples?" When the bewildered thief asked why, the officer replied, "You have one with queer seeds in your case." Now, 100 years after Schiltz's accidental discovery, the Musée Condé and Château de Chantilly are displaying the diamond publicly for the first time in a century. To prevent another theft, curators have partnered with the School of Jewelry Arts of Paris to create an identity card for the stone—a detailed scientific analysis documenting its chemical composition, clarity, and density. Should the diamond ever be stolen, cut, or reshaped, this record would help jewelers and authorities worldwide recognize it instantly.

The exhibit runs from October 17th through January 3rd, offering visitors a rare chance to see this legendary stone up close—and to appreciate the remarkable history contained within it.
quick_facts: Suzanne Schiltz, a Paris chambermaid, discovered the Grand Condé diamond inside an apple in 1926
The diamond was stolen from Château de Chantilly, about 30 miles north of Paris
Thieves took the diamond plus 74 other jewels using only a ladder
Valued at $3 million in the 1920s, yet thieves couldn't sell most pieces
The diamond goes on public display October 17th through January 3rd
